newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon sees no sign that Iraq targeted US jet.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon sees no sign that Iraq targeted US jet.

text.p: The United States on Sunday said it had no evidence that Iraq targeted the U.S. F-16 jet whose pilot fired on an Iraqi missile battery on Saturday after concluding he had been targeted by missile-tracking radar.

The Defence Department issued a statement late Sunday saying that "further analysis of Saturday's incident involving a U.S. aircraft over southern Iraq has not substantiated initial indications of Iraqi radar activity."

A Pentagon spokesman said an investigation was continuing into the incident and it was unclear whether the radar activity picked up by instruments aboard the Air Force F-16CJ aircraft was due to an equipment malfunction.
But he defended the pilot's actions and said he "acted appropriately" in accordance with the rules of engagement for western forces patrolling a no-fly zone over southern Iraq.
Those rules permit pilots to attack any radar site which is illuminating their aircraft in a threatening way.
Iraq denied the incident occurred at all.
A White House spokesman earlier said there was no sign that Iraq changed its policy of not firing at Western allied planes patrolling the no-fly zones over the country.

"There is not an indication at this point of any change in the position ... of the overall disposition toward the no-fly zone," spokesman Michael McCurry told reporters accompanying President Bill Clinton on a campaign trip in Florida.
The Iraqi News Agency on Saturday quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesman dismissing the White House statement as "false news" aimed at helping Clinton win re-election.
"Such American allegations are baseless. No incident of any kind has occurred in Iraq's airspace," the spokesman was quoted as saying.
"Fabricating this false news is part of the U.S. election campaign, the U.S. style," INA quoted him as saying.
The spokesman said Iraq was still committed to a decision not to fire at U.S. and allied jets patrolling the two no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.
The decision was taken in September after a confrontation with the United States because of Baghdad's backing of a Kurdish group against a rival in the north.
The United States responded by attacking southern Iraq with missiles and extending the southern no-fly zone for Iraqi planes to the outskirts of Baghdad.
The White House confirmed late on Saturday a Washington Times report on the missile incident.
It said the U.S. plane returned to base without incident. Clinton was informed of the incident, which took place about 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT) on Saturday, White House spokesman Barry Toiv said.
The F-16 pilot fired a single High-Speed Anti-Radiation Missile (HARM) at what he believed was a mobile surface-to-air missile battery.
